title: Myth - If We Supervise and Evaluate Teachers More Intensely, the Quality of Teaching Will Improve
author: DuFour, Richard
summary: A guest essay by Richard DuFour, hosted on Dave Stuart Jr's blog, attacking the accountability-era assumption that closer supervision and tougher evaluation of individual teachers will raise the quality of teaching. DuFour opens with the ambient rhetoric of failing schools, then argues the supervision remedy rests on two conditions that do not hold. The first is time: the average principal oversees twenty to forty teachers against a span of control of eight to ten in other professions, while carrying twenty-one distinct responsibilities that any crisis can derail. The second is expertise, and here DuFour uses his own experience as a high school principal with a history background who could not judge whether calculus, physics or auto mechanics lessons were pitched at appropriate rigor. He cites a research review concluding that leaders serious about school improvement should spend their time somewhere other than teacher evaluation. The closing move reframes the problem as a badly posed question, swapping monitoring of teaching for collective monitoring of student learning, which is the professional learning community logic DuFour built his career on. The piece is a compact argument against doubling down on a strategy that has already failed.
points: DuFour grounds the impossibility claim in arithmetic rather than sentiment, contrasting a principal's twenty-to-forty-teacher span of control with the eight to ten typical elsewhere and noting that three quarters of principals call the job too complex to do well.

The expertise objection is the sharper one: a principal trained in one discipline cannot tell whether content in calculus or physics is correct, let alone appropriately rigorous, so frequent observation buys volume of feedback without quality.
The essay's pivot is from monitoring teaching to monitoring learning, which relocates improvement work from the principal's clipboard to collective teacher inquiry into student results.
DuFour frames intensified evaluation as doubling down on a strategy already shown not to work, which reframes the policy debate as a sunk-cost problem rather than an implementation problem.
Useful as a counterweight in any conversation about observation cycles, walkthroughs or evaluation rubrics as school improvement levers.
quotes: It is conventional wisdom in the United States that our public schools are failing. This is the message that Americans have received, ad nauseam. Plug the phrase “failing schools” into the searchable database Nexis, and it provides 544 hits in newspapers and wire stories for the single month of January, 2012.

The effort to improve schools by supervising a faculty into better performance will only lead to higher levels of student learning if principals have the time and expertise to provide meaningful feedback to every individual teacher. There is no evidence that these conditions exist . The average principal oversees twenty to forty teachers compared to an eight- to ten-employee “span of control” in most other professions.

There is growing concern that the demands on principals have expanded beyond what can be expected of mere mortals. As Michael Fullan writes on the principalship, “New expectations have been added on to the traditional ones without any consideration of whether the new role in its entirety is feasible under the current working conditions faced by principals. The principalship is being placed in an impossible position.

But even if principals could somehow carve out time for the time-intensive process of observing and evaluating teachers on a much more frequent basis, they often lack the content and pedagogical expertise to offer meaningful feedback to teachers. As a former high school principal with a major in history, I had no clue whether or not the teachers I observed in a calculus, foreign language, physics, auto mechanics, or countless other courses were presenting content at the appropriate level of rigor.

One of the most comprehensive analyses of factors that improve schooling concluded “there is a robust body of empirical work that informs us that if school improvement is the goal, school leaders would be advised to spend their time and energy in areas other than teacher evaluation.” If current efforts to supervise teachers into better performance have proven ineffective (and they have), the solution is not to double down on a bad strategy and demand more classroom observations, tighter supervision, and more punitive evaluations.

The effort to improve schools through tougher supervision and evaluation is doomed to fail because it asks the wrong question. The question isn't, “How can we demand that principals do a better job of monitoring teaching?” but rather, “How can we collectively do a better job of monitoring student learning?
